Received: 07-12-2025; Accepted: 07-07-2026; Published online: 31-07-2026 © The Author(s) 2026, This article is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) Riassunto: Il presente contributo presenta i risultati della campagna 2024 dell’American Excavations at Morgantina: Agora Valley Project, concentrata sul Temenos sudoccidentale nell’agorà inferiore della città. Le indagini hanno chiarito alcuni aspetti della planimetria e della sequenza di sviluppo del complesso, che sembra aver preso forma in larga misura nel periodo successivo alla conquista di Morgantina da parte dell’esercito romano nel 211 a.C. La campagna ha inoltre prodotto importanti testimonianze relative ad attività dell’Antica Età del Bronzo al di sotto del Temenos ampliando le nostre conoscenze sull’occupazione protostorica all’interno e nei dintorni della valle dell’agorà di Morgantina. I depositi di frequentazione tarda, sigillati da strati di tegole crollate e murature collassate, documentano l’ultima fase d’uso e l’abbandono di parti del complesso nella prima età imperiale. Parole chiave: Morgantina, Temenos sudoccidentale, Sicilia romana, Antica Età del Bronzo, naiskos, trasformazione urbana.

Abstract: This report presents the results of the 2024 season of the American Excavations at Morgantina: Agora Valley Project, focused on the Southwest Temenos in the city’s lower agora. Excavations clarified aspects of the plan and phasing of the temenos complex, which appears to have largely taken shape in the period following Morgantina’s capture by Roman forces in 211 BCE. The season also produced important evidence for Early Bronze Age activity beneath the later precinct, expanding what is known about prehistoric occupation in and around Morgantina’s agora valley. Late occupation deposits, sealed by layers of fallen roof tiles and collapsed masonry, document the final use and abandonment of portions of the complex in the early Imperial period. Keywords: Morgantina, Southwest Temenos, Roman Sicily, Early Bronze Age, naiskos, urban transformation. Introduction The American Excavations at Morgantina: Agora Valley Project (AVP) is a long-term research project focused on Roman-era Morgantina, broadly defined as the period between the city’s capture in 211 BCE and the end of sustained occupation on Serra Orlando around 50 CE. Our present work investigates the so-called Southwest Temenos, a large area of around 650 m2, located in the city’s lower agora (Fig.1). Earlier fieldwork in the 1960s and 1980s revealed the partial footprint of a complex of yet unknown function that appears to have been occupied into the late 1st century BCE or early 1st century CE. In conducting new excavations to reveal and fully interpret the structures within the Southwest Temenos, AVP aims to provide new data from which we may improve our understanding of life at Morgantina in the centuries after Roman conquest. The 2024 field season was the third year of work for AVP and the second year of active excavation. Fieldwork took place between June 11 and July 5, with a team of 35 professionals, undergraduates, and graduate students participating in all aspects of the excavations and post-excavation research.1

The Southwest Temenos The first excavations in the area of the Southwest Temenos were conducted in 1962; it was during this campaign that portions of the complex’s western-most features and rooms were discovered. Subsequent excavations conducted in 1966, 1980, and 1981 were more circumscribed in scope, involving a limited number of saggi planned to answer specific questions concerning the extent of the complex. The decades-long history of intermittent excavation at the Southwest Temenos is more thoroughly discussed in a recently published article in the Memoirs of the American Academy in Rome.2 The eastern perimeter wall of the Temenos incorporates, or at least closely follows, the eastern wall of the West Granary, a building that appears to have been largely reduced to its foundations by the first decades of the 2nd century BCE.3 A similar chronological relationship is suggested by the northern wall of the Temenos, which cuts across the ramp that once led to the granary’s principal entrance. Since this intervention blocked access to the warehouse, its construction likely postdates the granary’s abandonment. These architectural relationships, together with the evidence from a saggio excavated in 1981 that revealed the foundations of the eastern perimeter wall, led previous excavators to date the spatial formalization of the Southwest Temenos to the 2nd century BCE.4

Altogether, the Southwest Temenos encompasses a number of discrete structures that were linked together by a series of pavements and enclosed within the stone perimeter wall (Fig. 2). Building A, a free-standing rectangular structure measuring approximately 6.0 m in width × 8.5 m in length, occupies a central position within the Temenos. The short sides of the building are oriented in an east–west fashion. About 2 m from the inner face of the building’s eastern wall runs a line of rubble that spans the width of the building. At present, it is not possible to say whether this line of stones, which measures approximately 85 cm in width, preserves the remains of a cross wall or is simply a stone scatter. Nonetheless, the consistency of its form and the fact that it appears to respect the orientation of the building’s east and west walls does cause us to lean tentatively toward the former interpretation. Future excavations will clarify this question. South of Building A lies the South Complex, another free-standing structure composed of at least five rooms. At the northern and southern extent of the western Temenos wall are two substantial water basins, constructed of large, cut-stone blocks and lined with hydraulic plaster. At present, one can find a variety of paved surfaces that connect these free-standing structures. We are still determining the relative sequencing of their installation. A pavement of thin, square bricks (ca.  32 cm x 32 cm x 5 cm) runs along the western side of the enclosure between the entrance to the Temenos proper and the North Basin. Although now badly damaged, it is clear that the bricks were originally aligned in careful fashion to follow the orientation of the western perimeter wall and the western facade of Building A. A second pavement, formed from a mixture of cobblestones and fragmentary terracotta bricks runs in an east-west fashion between Building A and the South Complex.

Previous AVP Fieldwork and Goals for the 2024 Season Following a brief 2022 season that focused on cleaning the architectural remains brought to light by earlier excavations, AVP recommenced systematic excavation inside the Temenos in 2023. Initially, our fieldwork sought to clarify the architectural layout of the complex and to identify areas most likely to preserve intact stratigraphic deposits. The results of the 2023 season are presented in detail elsewhere and, thus, are only briefly summarized here.8 Excavations in that year revealed the full extent of Building A and confirmed that it was a free-standing structure. Our work also brought to light previously unknown rooms within the South Complex, one of which (Room 4) contained a dense scatter of rubble overlying a well-preserved layer of fallen roof tiles.

In Room 2 of the South Complex, excavators discovered a small limestone statuette depicting a nude boy holding a dove, a type of votive sculpture attested in Hellenistic sanctuaries around the Aegean.9

The primary objectives for the 2024 season were to establish a more complete architectural plan of the Southwest Temenos and to better understand its development over time. To accomplish these goals, two large trenches and one smaller saggio were laid out in different parts of the complex (Fig. 3): Trench 155 was positioned to clarify the occupation history, architectural plan, and construction phases of the South Complex. This trench, laid out as a long rectangle aligned parallel to the walls of the South Complex, extended eastward from the western wall of the Temenos to a point beyond the known limits of the structure. It measured approximately 20 x 15 m, with the long axis oriented east–west. Trench 156 aimed to address outstanding questions regarding the date and, most importantly, the function of Building A. This trench (15 x 9 m) encompassed the entirety of Building A as well as a substantial area to its north and

Findings of the 2024 Field Season Work in and around Building A Our excavations inside Building A began at the point where the excavations of 1966 had stopped. A large saggio that bisected the interior of the building along its east–west axis was drawn to determine the phasing of the structure’s construction. Having been left exposed for almost six decades, the hard-packed soil that we first encountered (1156001) was contaminated and contained a number of different soil matrices without any clear divisions.10 Below this level, the stratigraphy encountered within the saggio dug in 2024 corresponds rather closely to the sequence encountered in the southeast corner of the building in 2023.11 The contaminated soil gave way to an extremely hard-packed yellowishbrown silty clay after ca. 10 cm of excavation. This layer (1156003) was substantial (approx. 39 cm in depth) and became more vibrantly yellow as excavations progressed. Notably, it was relatively devoid of cultural materials. The paucity of ceramic material and other artifacts warrants consideration but finds no immediate explanation. The gradual change of soil color and relative lack of inclusions suggest that the context was the product of a long-term natural deposition of soil rather than an intentional construction fill. Despite the overall scarcity of ceramics within the context, black gloss fine wares and fragments of overpainted coarse wares recovered from this layer provide a terminus post quem for the end of this period of accumulation around the late 4th or early 3rd century BCE. This context directly overlays a denselypacked layer of dark grayish-brown soil (Munsell 10YR 3/2) with a clay-rich loam texture, known colloquially as cioccolato on account of its color and dense compaction (1156015).12 Artifacts recovered from the cioccolato included numerous sherds of Castelluccian-style pottery (ca. 2400–1600 BCE), several worked stone scrapers and blades, and a stone abrader (Fig. 4).13 Our work revealed that the structure was built with foundations of variable depths that account for the gradual east-west slope of the hillside (Fig. 5). Along the west side of the building (i.e., farther up the slope of the hill), the foundations extend just over a meter below the putative floor level of Building A, as inferred from the elevation of a large threshold block (548.48 MASL) set in the center of the building’s western wall (Wall N). We can compare the depth of the foundations of Wall N (547.50 MASL) to those at the eastern-most extent of Wall Q, excavated in 2023, which extend for another ca. 60 cm below (546.93 MASL). At all points where our work encountered the foundations of Building A, the masonry rested within the densely-packed cioccolato soil (Fig. 6). Excavations outside the southeast corner of Building A revealed the very top of a foundation offset associated with the building’s southern wall (Wall Q) at 547.62 MASL, about 50 cm below the level of the adjacent rubble pavement (548.10 MASL). However, our excavations have not yet recovered sufficient diagnostic material in or around the building to offer a firm date for its construction.

*Fig. 6: South wall of Building A (Wall Q), looking south. The foundations of the wall cut into the black-brown soil of the cioccolato soil that defines the Early Bronze Age stratum in this zone of Morgantina. The original interior pavement of Building A is completely absent, presumably having been robbed out in antiquity or in the intervening centuries. Although we lack occupation assemblages from inside the structure, the siting and architectural form of Building A together suggest we may be dealing with a naiskos, or small temple. Similar buildings are attested elsewhere in Sicily, including at Morgantina itself.14 The current state of our findings does not enable much discussion of Building A’s superstructure or internal organization, although the visible cluster of stones that runs across the width of the building may be the remains of an interior cross wall. Our investigations to the east of Building A in 2024 identified a rectangular area of cocciopesto pavement (1156023) that extended eastward approximately 3.5 m from the building’s eastern facade. The upper surface of the cocciopesto is only sporadically preserved, but traces of the underlying pebble bedding are visible throughout. This paved area is bounded to the north and south by rubble walls projecting from the northeast (Wall Z) and southeast (Wall R) corners of Building A. Wall R was found to terminate in a large, dressed limestone block at which point another rubble wall (Wall S) extends perpendicular to it, running in a north–south direction. At present, it appears that this north–south wall originally defined the eastern limit of the cocciopesto surface, delimiting a small forecourt in front of Building A. Given that this feature was uncovered at the far eastern edge of the trench and in the final days of the 2024 campaign, defining the full extent of Wall S remains an objective for a future excavation season. It is now evident that Wall R was built to abut the eastern wall of Building A (Wall P) and was founded at a much shallower depth than the walls of Building A. It follows that Wall Z, the counterpart of Wall R to the north, along with the cocciopesto surface contained by the two walls represent a later architectural intervention, although we cannot presently say whether these construction phases were separated by an intervening period of years or simply by a matter of days. Northwest of Building A, excavations in Trench 157 focused on the small platform that ran along the east side of the North Basin (see Fig. 3). Our work in 2024 revealed that conservation of the basin’s features, conducted as part of the Princeton-led campaigns in the 1960s, included more extensive intervention than was previously understood. In particular, the large masonry blocks that comprise the basin’s eastern retaining wall appear to have been reconstructed.*

Work in and around the South Complex Investigations in the South Complex revealed evidence for occupation during the presumed final phase of ancient activity in the Southwest Temenos. This was particularly evident in Room 4, where excavations continued below the superimposed layers of collapsed rubble walls and terracotta roof tiles, which had been first exposed during the 2023 season (Fig. 7). Beneath the Laconian roof tiles (1155013), excavators encountered a layer of densely compacted, rich-brown soil (1155016) containing a range of materials and built features indicative of low-intensity occupation that stretched into the last decade of the 1st century BCE or early 1st century CE.

*Fig. 7: Layer of fallen roof tiles over Room 4 of the South Complex. Notable among these features was a small oven (1155038) situated against the interior face of the room’s northern wall (Wall L; Fig. 8). The oven rested directly on the room’s final floor, an improvised surface of medium-brown soil impacted with pebbles (1155037). The oven itself was constructed from a mixture of fragmentary terracotta bricks and rubble and built against stacked stones and a large terracotta water pipe. Excavations revealed a thin layer of ashy soil in and around the oven, which contained a notable concentration of burnt animal bone and the carbonized remains of olives, cereals, and a number of non-cultivated flowering plants. Elsewhere in the room were found a range of ceramic tablewares, further suggesting the space was in part a locus for food preparation and cooking, and a well-preserved iron billhook (inv 24-44; Fig. 9).15 The lower portion of a terracotta hip bath stood beside the oven, tucked into the northwest corner of the room. The function of this installation within the space remains uncertain. Although a piece of bathing furniture, the tub’s placement within the room renders its use in this fashion unlikely. It is possible that the hip bath was repurposed for another domestic function, perhaps related to water storage. Further excavation and analysis may help to clarify its use.*

The remains of a small oven, constructed of stones and fragmentary terracotta bricks, are visible as is a hip bath placed against Wall L. The ceramic assemblage and associated small finds from the floor deposits in Room 4 date almost exclusively to the period following the Roman siege of 211 BCE. Eleven bronze coins were found lying directly on the room’s beaten-earth surface (1155016) or in the soil that had accumulated immediately above (1155013); among this number were two Catanaean hexades (ca. 210–190 BCE), a Syracusan issue struck in the decades after 212 BCE, two Mamertine pentonkiai (ca. 212–200 BCE), a Romano-Sicilian semis minted at Panormos around the middle of the 2nd century BCE, as well as three bronzes of the HISPANORUM series, struck at Morgantina in the 2nd and 1st centuries (Fig. 10a-c). The latest coins from this assemblage date to the second half of the 1st century BCE; these are a Roman as issued by Sextus Pompey between 42 and 38 BCE and a Roman bronze struck at Agrigentum in 21 BCE under the name of the proconsul L. *Fig. 10: Selection of bronze coins found below the layer of fallen roof tiles in Room 4 of the South Complex. Excavations in Room 2 of the South Complex produced similarly interesting results. In the western half of the room, we began at the level identified in the 1962 campaign as the room’s final occupation surface. The previous excavators had stopped after removing a layer of collapsed roof tiles and a deposit of soil beneath it containing still more fallen tiles and stones. It soon became clear that this level did not represent a true occupation surface but rather soil that had accumulated just above it. Our excavations descended in short order onto a makeshift cooking platform constructed from repurposed fragments of large terracotta pan tiles (Fig. 11), which had been set directly on the room’s final occupation surface. Similar to the small oven in Room 4, the platform was covered by a layer of ash containing a dense concentration of animal bones, including remains of several galliformes (likely chicken) as well as wild game such as red deer and hare (Fig. 12).17 A secure terminus post quem for the installation of the cooking platform in Room 2 is provided by a fragment of a molded lamp found directly beneath the pan tiles (Fig. 13). The lamp is delfinoform and of the “Ephesus” type, with rings of egg-and-dart and bead-and-reel molded decoration.18*

*Fig. 11: Hearth or cooking platform constructed of repurposed pan tiles in Room 2 of the South Complex; looking east. Such lamps first appeared in western Anatolia in the early 2nd century BCE and were introduced into Italy by the late 2nd century BCE.19 Local production of such lamps is attested at the East Granary pottery workshop at Morgantina, where they were manufactured in large quantities ca. 100–50 BCE. Preliminary Phasing of the construction of the Southwest Temenos Following two seasons of excavation, we are now in a position to propose a preliminary sequence for the construction and occupation of the area that has come to be known as the Southwest Temenos. This phasing remains provisional, pending further excavation and the completion of ongoing study of the stratigraphic, material, and architectural evidence recovered to date. Phase 1: Early Bronze Age Occupation (2400-1600 BCE) Although not directly associated with the later function of the Southwest Temenos, the AVP excavations have uncovered substantial evidence for Early Bronze Age activity in this part of the agora valley. Given the significance of this material for our understanding of the earliest occupation at Morgantina, we have designated the evidence for prehistoric settlement activity as Phase 1. In the area of the Southwest Temenos, and more broadly throughout Morgantina’s agora valley, the earliest material remains are typically encountered within and immediately above the cioccolato soil, which formed prior to sustained human occupation at the site and is widely attested across the Serra

Phase 2: Late Classical and Early Hellenistic Activity (Late 4th to End of the 3rd Century BCE) Evidence for activity in the area of the Southwest Temenos during the Late Classical and Early Hellenistic periods remains notably limited after two seasons of AVP excavation. This scarcity is striking in light of the extensive construction documented elsewhere in Morgantina’s agora during the 3rd century BCE. We have nevertheless retained this period as a distinct phase, not because the excavations have thus far produced abundant evidence for activity in this sector of the agora, but because the limited remains that can be assigned to this horizon likely predate the more visible architectural interventions that followed in Phase 3. To date, the clearest evidence for Phase 2 activity comes from a small saggio excavated within the southeast corner of Building A in 2023.27 This sounding brought to light the remains of a coarse surface, probably once belonging to an exterior paving, composed of crushed yellow bedrock. Similar pavements formed of crushed yellow bedrock have been identified in the courtyards of two recently excavated 3rd-century houses at Morgantina.28 The pavement found buried inside Building A appears to have been cut in antiquity; the soil deposited over and around the cut surface contained only a small quantity of ceramic material, though the diagnostic forms that were recovered date broadly to the late 4th and 3rd centuries BCE. Although only a very limited portion of the crushed bedrock surface survives, we may cautiously associate it with the development of this portion of the agora in the middle decades of the 3rd century BCE, when major building projects transformed the surrounding civic landscape, including the nearby theater and West Granary. The evidence remains too sparse to reconstruct the function or organization of this area in detail, but it suggests that the zone later occupied by the Southwest Temenos was impacted in some way during Morgantina’s Hellenistic monumental building program. Future excavation will be essential for determining whether this activity represents an early stage in the formalization of the Temenos or part of a more extensive pattern of 3rd-century development in the southwestern agora. Phase 3: Monumental Construction and the Further Articulation of Space (ca. 200 – ca.35 BCE) The third phase of activity, broadly dated to the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, marks the period in which the Southwest Temenos first assumed its recognizable architectural form. It is to this phase that we tentatively attribute much of the visible architecture preserved in the area today, including the Temenos wall, Building A, the South Complex,

Although the precise chronology of each of these interventions remains to be clarified through further excavation, their architectural character and stratigraphic relationships allow a preliminary sequence of development to be proposed. A key chronological anchor for this phase is the construction of the Temenos wall (Walls A, B, D in Fig. 3). As stated above, since the northern arm of the Temenos wall blocks access to the West Granary, it is reasonable to suggest that this arm (and possibly the entire Temenos wall) was constructed after the West Granary went out of use - - an event that probably occurred ca. 200 BCE.29 The construction of the perimeter wall thus represents a decisive moment in the formal definition of the area, transforming what had previously been a more loosely organized zone at the edge of the civic center into a bounded architectural precinct. Building A appears to belong to the same general phase of monumentalization, although its exact place within the sequence remains unresolved. The building shares its orientation with the western arm of the Temenos wall, a relationship that suggests the two may have been conceived within the same broader planning horizon, if not constructed at precisely the same moment. This association is strengthened by the orientation of Building A in relation to the West Granary. If our identification of the structure as a small naiskos is correct, then its original eastward orientation would make best sense only after the West Granary had been dismantled or reduced to its foundations. Had the granary still been standing, the presumed façade of Building A would have faced directly toward the granary’s western wall, with little room for either approach or visibility. The removal of the granary, by contrast, would have opened the eastern side of the structure onto the newly reorganized space of the temenos. Several features support the interpretation that Building A was initially approached from the east. These include the orientation of the building itself and the discovery of a cocciopesto-paved platform at its eastern end, which may have marked or framed the original point of access. At a later point in time, however, access to the building appears to have been reoriented toward the west. The still-visible western entrance is marked by a large threshold block and a small portico formed by two polygonal columns. Although worn and damaged, these columns appear to have once belonged to the proskenion of the theater. Their reuse as architectural embellishment for Building A most likely occurred after the abandonment or dismantling of the theater, sometime in the late 1st century BCE. Determining the date and circumstances of this modification will be an important priority for future campaigns, since it may mark a late episode in the reconfiguration of the Temenos and its function. The earliest construction of the South Complex can also be assigned tentatively to Phase 3. In its first recognizable form, the complex consisted of a two-room unit composed of Rooms 1 and 5. This unit follows nearly the same axis as Building A, and the similarity in orientation suggests that the two structures may have been planned in relation to one another. Furthermore, the architectural layout and size of the Rooms 1/5 unit suggest the possibility that it functioned as a naiskos, like Building A. If this interpretation is correct, the earliest enclosed form of the Southwest Temenos may have contained two parallel structures set within the newly defined perimeter wall: Building A to the north and the Rooms 1/5 unit of the South Complex to the south.30 At a subsequent moment, the South Complex was expanded through the addition of three rooms to the north (Rooms 2–4). Their secondary character is indicated by the fact that their walls do not bond with Wall I, which they share with the earlier two-room unit, but instead about it. The expansion of the South Complex therefore seems to represent a later episode in the articulation of the Temenos. Together with the construction of the basins and the paved surfaces between Building A and the South Complex, these additions suggest that the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE witnessed not a single act of construction, but a sequence of interventions through which the Southwest Temenos was progressively enclosed, monumentalized, and reorganized.

Phase 4: Late Occupation (ca. 35/30 BCE to ca. 25 CE). The fourth phase of activity is represented most clearly by the deposits excavated in Rooms 2 and 4 of the South Complex during the 2024 season. These deposits appear to document a period of late and, arguably, temporary or expedient, occupation of the structure shortly before its abandonment and collapse. They are especially important because they preserve the most diagnostic assemblages yet recovered for the actual use of these spaces. At present, we associate this late occupation with the period following the destruction horizon of the late 30s BCE, which Shelley Stone has convincingly connected with Octavian’s campaigns of retribution against Sicilian communities that had supported Sextus Pompey during the civil war.31 The evidence from the South Complex thus belongs to a broader moment of post-conflict activity in Morgantina’s civic center. The clearest evidence for this final phase comes from Room 4. Complementing the picture of late 1st-century BCE activity suggested by the numismatic evidence (discussed above), the ceramic assemblage from this room includes a range of 1st-century forms. Particularly notable are thin-walled wares and several nearly complete cooking vessels with burned bases, which may have been used within the space not long before its abandonment (Fig. 15). Other finds include fragments of at least six cut-glass vessels, among them several pieces of a blue linear-cut bowl with an upright rim (inv. 24-29; Fig. 16).32 The thin-walled ceramics and glass fragments find close parallels in assemblages from Cosa, especially those dated to the final decades of the 1st century BCE and the opening decades of the 1st century CE.33 Among the most narrowly datable finds is a fragment of stamped Italian terra sigillata recovered directly from the floor level beneath the tile collapse (Fig. 17). The stamp is fully preserved and corresponds to a die associated with the potter C. Tap(urius?) (CVArr. no. 1897), who was active at Puteoli between ca. 10 BCE and 10 CE. This vessel provides one of the most precise chronological anchors for the final use of Room 4.  Although previously unattested at Morgantina, products of this potter, who appears to have specialized in conical and hemispherical cups, are well documented at other Augustan-period sites across the Mediterranean, including the veteran colonies at Neuss on the Rhine, Tarragona, Mérida, and Mirobriga in the Iberian Peninsula, as well as at Alexandria in Egypt.34

Yet, the fact that the destruction of the South Complex does not appear to have resulted from human violence does not mean that its end was either gradual or uneventful. Conclusion and Avenues for Future Research The results of the 2024 AVP season allow us to sketch a much fuller history of the Southwest Temenos (Fig. 19), from its prehistoric origins to its final abandonment in the early Imperial period. Excavations have found that the complex overlies an Early Bronze Age occupation horizon, marking the first prehistoric settlement yet identified in the agora valley and expanding the diachronic depth of activity on Serra Orlando. Above this early horizon, limited evidence for interventions in the late 4th or early 3rd century BCE signal occupation consistent with known developments elsewhere in the agora. Along with the Temenos wall, the construction of Building A was likely the earliest monumental intervention. Its orientation and form recommend the identification as a small temple or naiskos, and may be compared to a number of Roman-era podium temples from elsewhere in Sicily dated to the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE.35 The ongoing transformation of the Temenos in this period also saw the creation and reshaping of the South Complex as well as the installation of multiple pavements and water basins. Finally, late, low-intensity occupation so far identified in Rooms 2 and 4 of the South Complex anchors the last phase of activity in the Southwest Temenos to the closing decades of the 1st century BCE and the first decades of the 1st century CE.*
